mcqs.question: A feed requests page C1 for filter F1. Before it lands, the user switches to filter F2 and a live update for post P arrives. The list ends up showing P twice and a C1 page underneath F2 results. Which client rule prevents both symptoms?
options: Append any response with a 2xx status and keep the order the pages arrived in.
Tag each page with its query, drop pages for a stale query, and merge items by id in server order.
Replace the whole list with the newest page, so only one response is ever rendered at a time.
Sort the merged items by the time each page was received locally, newest first.
mcqs.explanation: Both symptoms are identity failures, not transport failures. A page is only valid for the query that produced it, and P is the same entity whichever path delivered it, so the client stamps every request with its query identity, discards pages whose query is no longer current (and resets the cursor for the new query, so C1's nextCursor is never reused), then merges by stable id and keeps the server's order. The strongest distractor is the 2xx option: it is the shortest path a naive fetch loop writes, but a 2xx only says that request succeeded for the query that was current when it was sent, never that the query is still current, and appending never deduplicates P. Replacing the list avoids duplicates by throwing away the pages already read and still renders a stale page; a local receive-time sort cannot dedupe, and it hands ordering to client clocks that disagree across devices and retries.

mcqs.question: An autocomplete takes `loadOptions(query, signal)` as a prop and aborts the previous request through its `AbortController` on every keystroke. One implementation resolves from an in-memory index and ignores the signal, and QA sees the older query's rows render after the newer query's rows. What is the correct fix?
options: Require every `loadOptions` to honour the signal; then the abort guarantees no stale result is applied.
Tag each request with a generation or its query and drop results that are no longer current.
Debounce the input harder so two requests for different queries cannot overlap.
Clear the list while a request is in flight so stale rows are never on screen.
mcqs.explanation: `AbortController` cancels fetch work — the request, body reads, streams (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController) — but the component's contract accepts any promise, and cancellation is best effort even for fetch: work already resolved, served from a cache, or produced by a non-fetch source still lands. Because the component owns the rendered result, it has to check identity at arrival: capture a per-request generation or the normalized query before the await and compare it before committing state. The strongest distractor is the 'honour the signal' option, because it is a real improvement and connection hygiene worth doing, but it moves the correctness requirement into every caller and still cannot cover a promise that resolved before the abort landed. Debouncing narrows the overlap window and cuts requests but does not order results, and clearing the list hides the stale render while destroying usable rows and flickering — the stale write still happens.

mcqs.question: A dashboard needs a server-to-client status stream and a button that acknowledges an alert. A teammate proposes `new EventSource('/alerts/stream')` for the stream plus an ordinary `fetch` POST for the acknowledgement. A reviewer objects that mixing the two is wrong and the feature should be one WebSocket. Which assessment is correct?
options: The `fetch` is the flaw: `EventSource` can send upstream messages on the same connection once the server enables it.
The split is sound: SSE is one-way and reconnects on its own; a WebSocket earns its cost when commands get frequent.
The reviewer is right: SSE cannot traverse proxies and does not reconnect, so one WebSocket is needed.
Neither works: a persistent connection cannot guarantee message order, so polling is the only safe option.
mcqs.explanation: SSE is a one-way channel: MDN states that you cannot send events from a client to a server, so a command needs another path and the POST is that path (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events). The trade-off is the usual one: SSE runs over ordinary HTTP and reconnects by itself, while a WebSocket is worth its connection state, backoff and resume code only when client commands are frequent or latency-critical. The strongest distractor is the 'EventSource can send upstream' option, because 'one connection is cleaner' is a reasonable instinct, but `EventSource` exposes no send method — it issues a GET and the response body is the entire channel, so no server setting adds an upstream direction. The proxy claim inverts the comparison: SSE is plain HTTP, generally easier to operate through proxies and load balancers than a protocol upgrade, though buffering proxies must be configured to flush. Ordering is a server-side sequence concern in every transport, not a reason to poll and pay the latency and load.

mcqs.question: Which state representation best avoids contradictory request flags?
options: `isLoading`, `isDone`, and `isError` with no invariant
A single status union with valid states
A copy of every prop in local state
One global boolean for all requests
mcqs.explanation: React recommends avoiding contradictory state; a status value makes impossible combinations harder to represent. Independent flags can drift, copied props go stale, and one global flag conflates unrelated requests.

mcqs.question: What is the primary reason to use IntersectionObserver for an infinite-feed sentinel?
options: It gives exact overlap pixels for every scroll frame
It asynchronously reports threshold crossings without manual scroll measurement
It guarantees that requests cannot overlap
It virtualizes the feed automatically
mcqs.explanation: IntersectionObserver asynchronously observes intersection changes and is suited to infinite scrolling. It does not provide exact pixel-overlap logic, request coordination, or virtualization by itself.

mcqs.question: A release report shows p75 field values for the mobile feed: LCP 2.1 s, INP 180 ms, CLS 0.08, TBT 540 ms, TTFB 1.3 s. A teammate says the page fails two Core Web Vitals. Which reading is correct?
options: Two failures: TBT at 540 ms and TTFB at 1.3 s both exceed the Core Web Vitals thresholds.
No failure: the set is LCP, INP and CLS, compared at p75, and all three are inside the good thresholds.
One failure: TBT is the field measure of responsiveness, and 540 ms is above the good threshold.
The report is incomplete: FID, not INP, is the interaction metric collected in the field.
mcqs.explanation: web.dev defines the current set as LCP for loading, INP for interactivity and CLS for visual stability, evaluated at the 75th percentile, with good thresholds of 2.5 s, 200 ms and 0.1 (https://web.dev/articles/vitals). Every number in the report is inside those, so there is no Core Web Vitals failure. TBT and TTFB are supporting diagnostics — TBT is a lab proxy for main-thread blocking and TTFB describes server response — which is exactly why they can look bad while the field CWV are good. The strongest distractor is the TBT option: it sounds like 'the responsiveness metric', but it is a lab measurement of blocking time, not the field interaction latency INP reports, so 540 ms indicts the lab trace rather than this p75 verdict. The FID option is the same confusion one generation back: FID was the earlier interactivity metric, and INP replaced it because FID only measured input delay. Counting diagnostics as CWV invents failures the page does not have.

mcqs.question: What should reconcile an optimistic chat message with its canonical server message?
options: The local array index
The sender's wall-clock timestamp
A client command ID echoed by the server
The DOM node identity
mcqs.explanation: A client ID lets the response or event match the pending command and avoids appending a duplicate. Array positions, local clocks, and DOM identity are unstable across retries, devices, and reordering.

mcqs.question: A teammate proposes storing the offline editor's operation queue in IndexedDB so that 'conflicts resolve themselves on reconnect'. Which review comment is correct?
options: IndexedDB gives transactional storage and versioned schemas; merge semantics come from the protocol.
A queue replayed in order is enough: deterministic replay resolves concurrent edits.
IndexedDB evicts on its own, so the queue needs no expiry or encryption policy.
IndexedDB writes are synchronous, so the queue must live behind a service worker.
mcqs.explanation: IndexedDB is the transactional, asynchronous object store that makes the ledger durable — snapshot plus queued operations, with a schema version (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IndexedDB_API) — and durability is the part it actually solves. Convergence is a different decision: either a central sequencer transforms each operation against the ones it did not see (OT), or the operations commute by construction (CRDT). A queue carries edits; it does not merge them. The strongest distractor is the replay-order option, because ordered idempotent replay is genuinely required and easy to mistake for sufficiency: an operation based on revision N that arrives after someone else advanced to N+1 is either rejected or silently overwrites, and replay cannot invent the transform. Eviction is real — storage is bounded, so the design needs expiry, cleanup, encryption for sensitive drafts and a logout path — and the synchronous claim is simply wrong: IndexedDB is async, and a service worker caches requests rather than running the editor's merge.

mcqs.question: A screen-reader user is reading older history in a chat. Every incoming message is announced immediately and the viewport jumps to the bottom on each arrival. Which change set fixes both symptoms?
options: Keep `aria-live="assertive"` and add `preventScroll` to the focus call, since silence would hide new messages.
Preserve focus and scroll position, announce 'N new messages' in a polite region, and offer a keyboard jump.
Move focus to the newest message on arrival so assistive technology reads it in context.
Drop the live region, because message bodies are already in the DOM and reachable by navigation.
mcqs.explanation: A live region exists to announce changes, so the fix changes what it announces and when: a polite region waits for a pause instead of interrupting, and a short status — '3 new messages' — carries the fact without reading every body over the text the user is currently hearing (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-live). The reading position stays, and the jump becomes deliberate: a keyboard-operable affordance moves focus when the user asks for it. The strongest distractor is the assertive-plus-`preventScroll` option, because it looks like the minimal fix that protects the scroll; but `preventScroll` only affects the focus call, the inserted message is still announced assertively over the user's current speech, and asserting every body is the loudest possible way to say 'something arrived'. Focusing the newest message steals the reading position and the screen-reader cursor, and removing the region leaves no signal at all: a durable message that is in the DOM but never announced is silent for someone who is not at the bottom.

mcqs.question: A de-DE build renders `You have 3 item(s)` from `t('youHave') + ' ' + count + ' ' + t('items')`, and formats a EUR amount by concatenating a hardcoded `$` with `amount.toFixed(2)`. Which fix is correct?
options: Add a singular branch (`count === 1 ? t('item') : t('items')`) and keep one formatted amount string per locale.
Use one message id with plural selection, and format the amount with `Intl.NumberFormat` for the active locale and currency.
Keep the fragments and fix the word order per locale in a config table, since order is the only difference.
Set `dir` from the locale and translate each fragment separately, since direction and translation cover a locale.
mcqs.explanation: Two different systems are being approximated with string assembly. A sentence containing a count is one message with plural selection: plural categories differ per language and the translation unit has to be the whole sentence with its placeholders, or translators cannot reorder, inflect or add categories. Money is a locale-sensitive format — separators, symbol placement, negative forms — which is what `Intl.NumberFormat` derives from a locale and an ISO currency code (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/NumberFormat); the machine value plus currency code stays separate from the rendered label. The strongest distractor is the singular-branch option, because it is the fix English developers ship and it looks disciplined: it hardcodes one language's category split into code, and the per-locale amount constant still hardcodes the symbol and the separators. A word-order table makes translators edit code; translating fragment by fragment leaves the assembly in code, which is the defect; and `dir` is layout direction, not translation — direction belongs to the document and to logical properties.

mcqs.question: A server-side table requests rows with sort S1, and before that response arrives the user switches to sort S2. Which client rule keeps the table from showing a mismatched page?
options: Abort the S1 request; once aborted, an S1 response can no longer reach the table, so no further guard is needed
Tag each request with its query identity, discard responses whose identity is not the current query, and reset the cursor when sort or filters change
Keep the cursor across the sort change because cursors are opaque and independent of the query, then append whatever arrives
Merge both responses and deduplicate by row id, since surviving rows are the same entities either way
mcqs.explanation: The table design is query state plus a selection model, and the server is authoritative for rows and ordering, so a page is only valid for the query that produced it: compare query identity before rendering, and reset or reconcile the cursor when the sort or filters change. The strongest distractor is the abort option: cancellation is best effort, and a response can already be resolved and parsed when the abort lands, so the identity check is still required. Keeping an opaque cursor across a sort change asks the server for the wrong window, and merging by id cannot repair wrong membership or wrong order.

mcqs.question: Users report that a large-file progress bar reaches 100% and then the upload still fails. Which progress model is correct for a resumable multipart upload?
options: Bytes sliced from the File and handed to fetch, aggregated as the loop advances
The sum of bytes in parts the server has confirmed, tracked per part identity
A timer-driven estimate that interpolates toward 100% while any request is open
The number of parts dispatched divided by the total part count, reported before each request returns
mcqs.explanation: Progress has to mean confirmed work: aggregate the bytes of parts the server accepted, keyed by stable part identity, so a retry does not double-count and a failure never shows completion. The strongest distractor is the dispatched-bytes option because it is what a naive fetch loop naturally produces, and it is exactly what makes the bar reach 100% before the server has durably accepted the data. Timer estimates and pre-response part counts are optimistic in the same way.

mcqs.question: The UI evaluated a capability as allowed and showed an Edit action, but the API answers with a structured 403. What is the correct client behavior?
options: Retry with backoff, because a 403 can be a transient authorization failure like a 429
Surface the denial as a recoverable state, invalidate the cached capability for that user, tenant, or resource, and refetch the policy
Treat the 403 as a server defect, keep the action visible, and let a later request correct the state
Hide the whole route and sign the user out, since any authorization failure means the session is invalid
mcqs.explanation: Authorization is a server-owned policy: a structured 403 is authoritative, so the UI reports the denial and reconciles the capability it cached, then re-renders from fresh policy data. The strongest distractor is the retry option because 403 looks similar to other status codes in a generic error path, but 403 is a decision, not a transient condition, so retrying just repeats the denial. Keeping the action visible dismisses the only authoritative signal, and a global sign-out overreacts to one denied action.

mcqs.question: A dashboard renders six independent widgets. One widget's upstream is down and the session token has expired. How should the shell respond?
options: Load all six with Promise.all and render one dashboard-level error as soon as the first request rejects
Let each widget settle independently; keep the isolated upstream failure local with its own retry, and escalate the shared auth failure to a session-level state
Block the shell until all six resolve so the layout never changes, then render once
Retry every widget with unbounded backoff and keep the global spinner until all six succeed
mcqs.explanation: Each widget is its own query boundary with its own loading, stale, empty, and error states, so a single broken upstream cannot erase five working widgets, while a failure shared by every request such as an expired session is escalated once. The strongest distractor is Promise.all: it fails fast and it is shorter code, but it converts one widget's outage into a total dashboard outage and gives the user no working data. Blocking the shell and unbounded global retries both destroy partial availability for the same reason.

scenarios.prompt: A searchable feed uses the hook below. Users report that results for an older query sometimes replace results for a newer query. Propose the architecture and state transitions you would use.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Keep the visible input separate from debounced remote work. On each issued query, increment a generation and create a local controller; capture both in the async operation. Abort the previous request, but before committing loading, success, or error, verify that the generation and normalized query are still current. Treat an abort as non-user-visible cancellation, handle empty input separately, and expose loading, empty, and error states accessibly. If results are cached, define freshness and privacy rules. The component should own only interaction state; a query/cache layer can own request lifecycle and reuse results.
rubric: Separates input state from debounced request state
Uses abort plus generation or query identity checks
Handles empty, loading, error, and cancellation states
Defines cache freshness and privacy rather than caching blindly
Keeps the component contract and ownership narrow

scenarios.prompt: A chat client ships with the types and handlers below. After a reconnect, users see their own last message twice; a send that times out disappears from the thread; and on a slow connection a reply sometimes renders above the message it answers. Review the code, name the defects, and specify the protocol and state model you would ship.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Separate the three symptoms before designing anything, because each has a different cause and each maps to a line of this code.

1. The duplicate is an identity failure. `clientId` is generated and used as the local key, then dropped from the wire payload, so the server has nothing to echo; the broadcast creates a second row keyed by `event.id`, and `onEvent` appends instead of reconciling. The command must carry the client id, and both the ack and the broadcast must return it. Reconciliation is then a merge from pending to canonical by that id, applied idempotently, because the same message can arrive as an ack, as a broadcast, and twice after a retry.

2. The disappearing send is a state failure. The row exists only as a local push with `state: "pending"`; nothing transitions it to failed or unknown, and because the server never receives the client id, no server copy can ever confirm or replace it. Any path that rebuilds the list from the server — the reconnect refetch in particular — has no entry for that key, so the text is simply gone. Model four states: pending (local copy only), accepted (canonical id and sequence), failed (recoverable text with retry and delete), and unknown (no acknowledgement after a timeout — ask the server whether that client id exists, then accept or fail). A failed send keeps its text; silence is not a state the UI can render.

3. The out-of-order reply is an ordering failure. `seq` is declared on the event and never read, and `push` preserves arrival order, so a reply that took a slower path renders below the message it answers. Order by the per-conversation `seq`, never by arrival or by a device clock. If an event arrives with a missing predecessor, buffer it, wait a bounded time, then fetch history after the last applied sequence and apply the result idempotently.

The protocol I would ship, per conversation:

- client → server: `{ type: "message.send", clientId, conversationId, text }`
- server → sender: `{ type: "message.ack", clientId, message: { id, seq, createdAt, text } }`
- server → conversation: `{ type: "message.created", message: { … } }`
- client → server on open: `{ type: "resume", conversationId, afterSeq }`

Retry reuses the same `clientId`, so a resend is deduplicated server-side instead of creating a second message. Retries are bounded with backoff and jitter for transient failures; a 4xx (validation, no longer a participant) stops the retry and surfaces a terminal failure. Reconnect keeps `lastAppliedSeq` and a bounded event buffer; when the gap exceeds the buffer, refetch a snapshot rather than replaying unbounded history. The client stores a normalized map by canonical id plus an ordered index by `seq` — not the canonical history, which stays on the server.

On the UI side, a reader who is not at the bottom must not be scrolled or focused: count new durable messages, announce 'N new messages' politely, and move focus only when the affordance is activated. Typing and presence stay ephemeral, expire on their own, and never enter the message list.
rubric: Traces the duplicate to `clientId` being generated locally but dropped from the wire payload, and to `onEvent` appending instead of reconciling by identity.
Defines the envelopes: command with `clientId`, ack carrying both `clientId` and canonical message, broadcast carrying `id` and per-conversation `seq`.
Models pending / accepted / failed / unknown and keeps a failed send recoverable with an idempotent retry that reuses the same client id.
Makes reconnect resume from the last applied sequence with a bounded buffer and a snapshot fallback, and applies events idempotently.
Preserves reading position and announces a concise new-message status instead of force-scrolling or focusing on arrival.

scenarios.prompt: One route policy was applied to a public article page and to an authenticated dashboard. Field data now shows: the article's p75 LCP is 4.6 s on mid-range Android over 4G and the crawler records an empty `#root`; the dashboard keeps serving last week's widget data after a user's role changes; and its 40-row activity list — virtualized, as the config says — breaks in-page find and moves focus onto the wrong row after a filter. Review the config, name what each symptom indicts, and give the per-route policy you would ship with its acceptance criteria.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Two properties are being decided once for two surfaces that disagree about them: who builds the document, and how long data stays valid. A shared default is the first defect — not the individual values — because rendering strategy and cache policy are per route and per kind of data.

Article. `csr` puts the wrong side of the trade on a page whose content is identical for every reader. The HTML contains an empty root, so nothing is indexable until JS runs, and the LCP element waits for bundle download, parse and execution on a mid-range device; 4.6 s is that chain, not the network alone. The content changes when editors publish, which is the prebuild case: render it at build/publish time, serve it from an edge cache and revalidate on the publish event, and hydrate islands only for the parts that need interaction. SSR is acceptable too; the requirement is that the LCP element lives in the initial HTML.

Dashboard. The shell and the widget data have different freshness. Server-render the shell — layout, navigation, skeletons — so first paint is not blank, then fetch each widget in the client, because the data is authenticated and per user. `cacheTtl: "forever"` is the defect behind the stale widgets: freshness is a property of the data, and a cache key that ignores user, tenant and role serves one context's data to another. Key entries by query plus scope, invalidate on role change, login/logout and tenant switch, and where staleness is acceptable use background revalidation with a visible 'as of' timestamp. Authorization is server-owned: the client renders what the policy says and reconciles on the structured denial instead of pinning a decision forever.

Virtualization. A 40-row list is the case where windowing costs more than it saves. Unmounted rows are absent from in-page find, and restoring focus by index lands on whatever now occupies that slot. Keep the list mounted; when a route really holds thousands of variable-height rows, virtualize that surface only, keep DOM order and accessible names correct, restore focus by item id, and give the user a way to reach the full content.

Acceptance criteria, per route: field p75 LCP/INP/CLS with the article's LCP element present in the initial HTML; a crawler or `view-source` check that the article body is in the document; an authorization test where a revoked role stops seeing widget data after the mutation rather than after a TTL; keyboard and in-page-find checks on both lists; and lab checks per route in CI, so the policy is a gate instead of a comment in a config file.
rubric: Names the shared default config as the defect and decides rendering per route from requirements — indexability and identical content versus authenticated interaction.
Moves the article's LCP element into the initial HTML (prebuild/SSR plus edge cache revalidated on publish) instead of tuning CSR.
Treats freshness as a property of the data: scope-aware cache keys and invalidation on role, tenant and session changes.
Rejects virtualization for the 40-row list and names its concrete costs — in-page find and focus restoration by item id.
Gives verifiable acceptance criteria: field p75 CWV per route, an HTML/crawler check, an authorization test, and keyboard plus find checks.

scenarios.prompt: Large media uploads fail on flaky mobile networks and users cannot resume after a reload. Review the implementation below, name the design defects, and propose the contract and state model for a resumable upload that supports progress, cancellation, and recovery.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Start by separating the protocol from the UI. This loop has no upload identity, so a retry after a network drop re-sends part zero and the server has no way to know what it already holds; each POST is an anonymous file, so a partial run leaves orphaned objects. Progress is computed from dispatched parts rather than confirmed bytes, which is why the bar reaches 100% before completion. Nothing is persisted, so a reload starts over, and cancellation is absent: there is no abort signal and no abort/cleanup call, so abandoned uploads keep billing and consuming quota.

A resumable multipart design: (1) initialize an upload with file name, byte size, content type, part-size policy, and a client checksum, and receive an upload id plus the part size the server will enforce (S3 multipart works this way: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html); (2) slice the File into numbered parts of that size; (3) PUT each part to `/uploads/{uploadId}/parts/{n}` with the body, bounded concurrency (three or four is enough on mobile), and an AbortSignal; (4) the server returns a stable identity per part, an ETag or checksum, and the PUT is idempotent, so re-sending a completed part is safe and the response tells the client whether it already existed; (5) persist `{uploadId, partSize, completedParts: Map<number, etag>, fileFingerprint}` in IndexedDB with a schema version and an expiry, so a reload or a crash resumes from the ledger instead of from zero; (6) complete with the ordered part list, and let the server validate authorization, declared size, type, and final integrity, returning a structured conflict if parts are missing; (7) abort calls a server endpoint that discards the parts and clears local metadata, and any lifecycle rule expires incomplete uploads server-side.

Progress becomes the sum of confirmed part bytes over the declared total, so it never regresses and never lies. Retries are bounded with backoff and jitter for transient failures only (network errors, 5xx, timeouts); a 4xx such as an expired upload id or a size rejection stops the retry and surfaces a recoverable failure state, typically re-initializing a new upload while keeping the file local. For transfer-level progress events the browser exposes `XMLHttpRequest.upload` progress (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest); `AbortController` cancels fetch work (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController) but does not by itself make an upload resumable, which is why the ledger and part identities are the actual mechanism. Model the client state as `idle | initializing | uploading | paused | completing | done | failed`, with a per-part state of pending, in-flight, confirmed, or failed, and make multi-tab or duplicate-tab resume safe by treating the ledger as owned by one active uploader per file fingerprint.
rubric: Identifies the missing upload identity and the anonymous per-part POST as the reason nothing can resume
Proposes a multipart contract with numbered parts, stable part identities, idempotent retries, and a server-side complete/abort
Tracks progress as confirmed bytes and models explicit states instead of one percentage
Persists upload metadata with expiry and privacy rules so a reload or crash resumes
Bounds concurrency and retries, separates transient from terminal failures, and cleans up cancelled uploads
